Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty Images House prices UK houses near top state secondary schools cost £40,000 more, research reveals Premium of nearly 10% paid by housebuyers comparable with cost of a cheaper private school over seven years Rob Davies Mon 31 Aug 2026 19.01 EDT Last modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A house near a top state secondary school costs an extra £40,000 on average, according to research that reveals education premiums that rank alongside some private school fees. The average property in a postcode district that includes a top 50 state secondary commands a price tag of £415,791, compared with £375,217 across the wider local authority areas in which those schools are located, a UK-wide analysis by the estate agent Yopa found. The £40,574 extra, a premium of about 11%, can be compared with an average annual fee of £23,000 charged by private schools, according to the Good Schools Guide. However, some charge less than £6,000 a year, indicating that over seven years of secondary education parents could end up paying a similar sum to the average extra cost of a house near a top state school. The increased price tag for such properties varies significantly across the country, according to the research, although individual cases can be less informative than the overall average, due to local market factors. Bishop Vesey’s grammar school in the well-to-do West Midlands town of Sutton Coldfield tops the table of schools where buyers are likely to pay much more than in the surrounding area. Homes across the B74 postcode district go for an average of £509,964, a premium of £275,814 compared with the average of £234,150 in Birmingham, which includes more economically deprived areas. In London, the biggest premium is paid by people living close to Henrietta Barnett school, a grammar academy for girls. The average property across its NW11 postcode is valued at 37% more than in the rest of the surrounding borough of Barnet, equivalent to an additional £354,288. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion UK house prices flat in July, says Lloyds, as buyers struggle with affordability Read more However, there are some outliers to the trend. Across the postcode district home to Reading school and Kendrick school, the average property costs £276,870. That is £84,373 below the wider Reading average of £361,243. Verona Frankish, the chief executive of Yopa, said: “For many homebuyers with children, the quality of local schools is one of the most important considerations when deciding where to live and, with the new school year approaching, education will be front of mind for many families considering their next move.” Separate research reveals that in London, homebuyers with children who go to a nearby private school are opting in to a double whammy of extra costs, with properties near a top fee-paying establishment – which are often located in the most upmarket areas – going for premiums of up to 77%. Queen’s college, London, tops the table. Homes across the W1 postcode command an average price of £1.92m compared with the wider Westminster average of £854,198. Westminster school and Francis Holland school, Sloane Square follow. Both are located within the SW1 postcode, where the average property price stands at £1.49m, a premium of 54.5% compared with Westminster as a whole. https://www.politico.eu/article/marine-l.text: PARIS — Jordan Bardella spent months preparing to replace Marine Le Pen as France’s far-right presidential candidate. Now he has a different challenge: falling back in line behind her. In just a few days, the two leaders of the National Rally have struck competing notes on sensitive issues, from pensions and the high-profile departure of a top adviser to a long-standing proposal by Le Pen to ban hijabs. Once seen as his party’s most likely candidate, the 30-year-old member of the European Parliament had to step aside in early July after a court shortened Le Pen’s sentence for embezzlement of EU funds, allowing her to run. Advertisement Advertisement In positioning himself for a possible campaign, Bardella had tried to soften the National Rally’s image, especially on the economy, in an attempt to appeal to more moderate voters the party will likely need to win next year’s presidential election. Le Pen is leading the polls in a crowded field, making it likely she will win the first round of the French election and advance to the two-candidate runoff — a feat she has accomplished twice before, only to lose to French President Emmanuel Macron. Tensions between the two have bubbled just below the surface in the weeks since Le Pen reasserted herself as the party’s presidential standard-bearer. On the day after the July verdict, Bardella stood stern-faced beside his mentor as she sought to cast their relationship as a partnership, with Le Pen as the candidate for France’s highest office and her protégé as her pick for prime minister, a much less powerful role. Bardella did not attend a presidential debate last week in which Le Pen doubled down on a campaign promise to roll back a key element of Macron’s pension reform and allow workers to retire at 62. He had openly questioned that policy earlier this year as part of his campaign to cast himself as a fiscally responsible leader. Advertisement Advertisement As Le Pen outlined her economic agenda at the debate, news broke that François Durvye, one of her key economic advisers and a leading advocate of fiscal discipline, was leaving the campaign. The former financier left after he had reportedly pushed Bardella to rebel and run instead of Le Pen. He also made clear privately and publicly that he did not feel able to defend the party’s positions on the economy. Pressed by reporters at a campaign event, Bardella described the departure as Durvye’s “personal decision” — seemingly contradicting Le Pen, who said on the sidelines of the debate that it had been “her wish.” Jean-Philippe Tanguy is pictured in the National Assembly in Paris on July 6, 2026. | Julien de Rosa/AFP via Getty Images Tensions were also on display this week after one of Le Pen’s top lieutenants, MP Jean-Philippe Tanguy, said that wearing the hijab in public would become a fineable offense if she took office, a controversial measure rivals say is unconstitutional. The day after, Bardella appeared to downplay the proposal, saying instead it would be up to French voters to decide via a proposed referendum, which Le Pen later said would include a series of measures that would “fight Islamist ideology.” National Rally officials have sought to downplay the disagreements between the two leaders. Advertisement Advertisement “There was an internal debate, and the conclusion was the proposed hijab ban,” said Laurent Jacobelli, a member of Parliament and a spokesperson for the National Rally. “It was settled with everyone’s agreement, Jordan included.” “There was agreement on the ban itself,” Jacobelli added. “What got debated was the how … There were no tensions.” Alexandre Loubet, a member of Parliament for the National Rally, acknowledged that the party was still discussing the details of some elements of the platform. “There are still many things that need deciding,” Loubet told POLITICO at an agricultural fair where Bardella was making an appearance Saturday. Loubet acknowledged the party was still working out the numbers to pay for the cost of rolling back Macron’s reform. Le Pen has promised to present a plan this fall to cut some €125 billion in spending. Bardella, Loubet said, will be “her first support … in the media, on the field, to broaden the [future] majority.” Advertisement Advertisement Not everyone at the fair was convinced. “Bardella would have been a better candidate,” said Kaelig Le Bris, a 41-year-old garbage collector who had come to see him. Le Bris said he was a fan of Le Pen but “a guy like him at the helm of the country, that would have been something.” During his appearance at the fair, Bardella repeatedly batted down reporters’ questions about the disagreements between him and Le Pen. “I will campaign whatever happens,” he said. “Alleged hurt feelings don’t matter.”

https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-budge.text: BRUSSELS — Europe will lose out because of €159 billion in cuts to the bloc’s next long-term budget, the European Commission has warned days before EU leaders gather in Brussels for talks on the bloc’s future spending plans. In an unusual attack, the Commission told governments that scrapping billions from several rainy-day funds will leave Europe less equipped to deal with crises during the next seven-year budget cycle, said four EU diplomats briefed on the talks, granted anonymity to speak freely about confidential discussions. The Commission’s top budget official, Stéphanie Riso, delivered the warning to the EU’s 27 ambassadors during a closed-door meeting on Sunday, a day after the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, which is steering the talks, proposed cutting around 8% from the bloc’s total budget from 2028 to 2034. Advertisement Advertisement The Commission is “very concerned about cuts to flexibility,” said one of the EU diplomats. As a result of the changes, “we will have no ways left to help farmers and regions when crises hit, because of climate change or geopolitical tensions,” they added. EU ambassadors gathered to discuss the Irish plan , which envisages cuts of €159 billion in current prices from the Commission’s nearly €2 trillion proposal. Of that amount, €38 billion was cut from foreign aid, €75 billion was axed from competitiveness, and at least €22 billion was slashed from rainy-day funds. But even those reductions were criticized as insufficient by a German-led group of states pushing for cuts of several hundred billion. During the closed-door meeting, a rival bloc of 17 countries, known as the Friends of Cohesion, welcomed the fact that the Irish presidency had spared agriculture and regional payments from cuts. EU governments are racing to finalize a deal on the budget among themselves by the end of the year — before elections in France, Italy and Poland that threaten to disrupt the negotiations. A leaders’ summit on Thursday and Friday will give early signals as to whether the end-of-year deadline is achievable — or whether leaders should start preparing contingency plans. Advertisement Advertisement One EU diplomat said the pressure is now on those leaders: “What could make a difference is if Friedrich Merz and Emmanuel Macron show up, hand-in-hand, and say we live in a new world.” Cuts to the future The Commission warned that cuts such as those put forward by Ireland will shrink the next budget — excluding repayments to post-Covid debt — below the current one. The cuts overwhelmingly affect EU-wide priorities such as competitiveness, defense and foreign aid while leaving traditional policies untouched such as agriculture and regional payouts, which make up almost half the budget. Friedrich Merz and Micheál Martin during a press conference in Dublin on July 28, 2026. | Paul Faith/AFP via Getty Images The changes undermine the Commission’s proposal, which envisaged more flexibility and steered hundreds of billions of euros toward new priorities. In a further setback for the Commission, Ireland also downsized — or even scrapped — several financial cushions to shelter EU countries from unforeseen events such as natural disasters or public health emergencies. The EU executive argues these changes will make spending in the next budget more rigid than in the current one — and potentially warrant a midterm review of the budget further down the line. Advertisement Advertisement However, Ireland’s Europe Minister Thomas Byrne disputed this claim in a press conference on Saturday, saying the budget proposal “offers increased flexibility ... in response to the clear call from member states for a simplified and more flexible, modern [budget].” Another source of tension in the next budget came from Ireland’s watering down the link between EU payouts and economic reforms. The Commission has repeatedly defended using regular budget payments as a carrot to nudge governments to undertake reforms that will make them more competitive. However, Ireland’s ambassador to the EU, Aingeal O'Donoghue, said during the meeting that the new text will not link EU cash disbursements and “fiscal reforms,” according to one of the diplomats.

https://www.budapesttimes.hu/world/a-tal.text: The Budapest Times A tale of two extraditions: same case, same court, very different verdicts The Paris prosecutor's office on Wednesday requested the extradition to Hungary of a Syrian antifascist who is accused of attacking people considered far-right in Budapest in February 2023, causing serious injuries. The investigative chamber of the Paris Court of Appeal, which handles extradition cases, will decide on 25 November whether to extradite Zaid Altayeb, who has been granted refugee status in France, to Hungary. “There are sufficient guarantees to request the immediate extradition of Zaid Altayeb to Hungary,” the prosecutor said on Wednesday at the final hearing on the European arrest warrant, according to AFP. According to the representative of the prosecution, the independence of the judiciary in Hungary has been strengthened in recent months. The Hungarian authorities are requesting the extradition of the 23-year-old Syrian Zaid Altayeb in order to hold him accountable for his role in the violent clashes that took place in Budapest in February 2023. The man, along with several of his associates who are also wanted by the Hungarian authorities, came into conflict with participants in a demonstration held on the so-called Day of Honour. Laurent Pasquet-Marinacce, the activist’s lawyer, disagreed with the prosecutor’s position at the hearing. In his view, his client is an “ideal culprit constructed in a methodical manner,” which is why “the risk of an unfair trial has not disappeared” in Hungary. The lawyer stated that he had been present in Budapest at the Budapest Regional Court of Appeal’s final sentencing hearing on 30 September in the antifa case, where the sentence of the fourth-ranked defendant, the German Maja T., was reduced by the court from the eight-year prison sentence handed down at first instance to seven years. The lawyer said that he had “witnessed an inhumane humiliation, where Maja T.’s hands and feet were in very tight restraints.” “A change of government does not erase 15 years of destruction of everything that makes a rule-of-law state a rule-of-law state,” said the legal representative. Zaid Altayeb, who is free, believed that “all progress takes time, and the detainees will be the last to benefit from it — and I, as a Syrian, will perhaps be the last among the last.” In the same case, French justice rejected in April 2025 the extradition to Hungary of Rexhino Abazaj, a 32-year-old Albanian antifascist activist known by the nickname Gino. The president of the extradition division of the Paris Court of Appeal, when announcing the decision, cited the “dangers” in Hungary of violations of the rights guaranteed by the articles of the European Convention on Human Rights relating to the prohibition of torture and the right to a fair trial, citing as examples “cruel treatment” in prison and the uncertainty of ensuring a fair trial. The Albanian man was subsequently also requested by Germany, for the same acts as those cited by Hungary, and this latter request was approved by the court of appeal on 19 August, then confirmed by the Court of Cassation on 30 September.
